extracted.intended_audience: general public and students learning about how scientific peer review and publication work
extracted.subtask_description: A concise set of criteria describing what peer review is intended to check in scientific manuscripts (the standards manuscripts must meet to be accepted by peer-reviewed journals) and how the review process functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum standards for scientific quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review helps provide assurance that published research meets minimum standards for scientific quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review typically involves experts vetting a submitted article and advising editors; only articles that meet good scientific standards are accepted for publication. The process is time-consuming and competitive (many journals accept a small percentage of submissions). Peer review provides a trusted form of scientific communication but is not a guarantee of correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and build upon other work in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Only articles that acknowledge and build upon other work in the field are accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should situate their study within the existing literature — citing relevant prior work and showing how the new study relates to, extends, or challenges that work. This demonstrates awareness of context and prevents reinventing or misrepresenting prior findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical reasoning and well-designed studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should rely on logical reasoning and well-designed studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers and editors expect clear, logically consistent arguments and appropriate study design (controls, sampling, experimental setup, analytic plan). Good experimental design and reasoning reduce bias and increase the credibility of conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be backed up with evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must back up claims with evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions need to be supported by data, analyses, and appropriate interpretation. Evidence should be presented clearly so reviewers can assess whether the claims follow from the data; transparency in methods and results aids verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation by expert peers in the same field
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors send the article to several other scientists who work in the same field (the 'peers' of peer review) to provide feedback and recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer reviewers evaluate subject-specific aspects such as methodology, novelty, significance, and interpretation. Their feedback informs the editor's decision to accept, request revision, or reject a submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision and resubmission based on reviewer feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may revise their article and resubmit it for consideration following reviewer feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review is often iterative: reviewers' comments can require changes to analyses, additional experiments, clarification of arguments, or rewriting. Successful publication commonly depends on authors' willingness and ability to respond constructively to critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication is trustworthy but provisional (not necessarily correct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer-reviewed work isn’t necessarily correct or conclusive, but it does meet the standards of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication signals that a study met the community's standards at the time of review, but subsequent work may confirm, refine, or overturn published findings. Consumers of research should treat published results as reliable to a degree but open to revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicability and follow-up as part of scientific scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: After publication, the scientific community may incorporate the work into established knowledge, build on it further, figure out why it is wrong, or try to replicate its results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replication and independent verification are key mechanisms for testing published claims. A study's long-term acceptance depends not just on peer review but on its reproducibility and how it withstands further scrutiny.
